title: The Covenant Test: Why Stocking Up for Christmas Can Quietly Breach a Loan Agreement
excerpt: Debt rises the moment Christmas stock is funded, but the sales that justify it land weeks later. If a bank covenant test falls in that gap, a strong business can look stretched on paper.
content:
By mid November, plenty of owner-led businesses on the east coast have already drawn on an overdraft, an equipment loan or a freshly increased facility to get stock on the shelf, trades booked or staff rostered before the busiest trading window of the year. The decision feels straightforward. More stock means more sales, and more sales means a stronger result to show the bank at the next review.

What gets missed, almost every time, is the covenant clause sitting quietly inside the facility letter. It was read once at settlement and rarely looked at again. That clause gets tested against a set of numbers calculated on a specific date, and that date often lands in the gap between the money going out the door and the sales coming back in. A business can be genuinely strong and still trip a covenant simply because of when the test fell.

This is not a sign anything has gone wrong. It is a timing mismatch that catches confident, well-run businesses more often than struggling ones, because it is the confident ones drawing down extra funding ahead of a peak trading period.

Why the Test Date Matters More Than the Trend

Most SME banking facilities carry at least one financial covenant, commonly a leverage ratio comparing total debt to EBITDA, an interest cover ratio, or a current ratio comparing short-term assets to short-term liabilities. These are tested at fixed intervals, usually quarterly or against trailing twelve month figures, rather than against the trajectory the business is actually on.

The trouble is that debt moves the moment it is drawn. EBITDA moves only once the stock or capacity that debt paid for has converted into sales and margin. Draw down extra funding in October or November to build Christmas stock, and the debt side of the ratio lifts immediately. The EBITDA side will not reflect the benefit until December's trading result is actually in the accounts, which for a trailing twelve month calculation can be months away. Depending on the covenant's test date, the business can show up temporarily worse geared than it has been all year, in the exact month it is about to have its best result.

The Stock-to-Sales Lag Banks Don't See

The pattern across owner-led businesses that stock seasonally, hospitality, retail, building suppliers, importers, is remarkably consistent. The cash and debt commitment for Christmas trading lands in October and November. The sales and margin that justify it land in December and January. A covenant test sitting on a calendar date in between sees only the cost side of that equation.

Nobody at the bank is trying to catch a business out here. Covenant testing is mechanical, and a relationship manager working from a trailing twelve month spreadsheet has no visibility into the fact that four weeks of strong trading are about to land. That is a conversation that has to happen from the business's side, and it has to happen before the test date, not after a breach notice arrives.

What to Do Before the Test, Not After

The fix is not complicated, but it does need to happen early. Model the covenant position before drawing down additional funding, not after. Know the test date and what the ratio will look like on that date given what has already been committed. If headroom is tight, a short conversation with the lender ahead of time, with the forecast attached, almost always lands better than an unplanned breach notice during the business's busiest trading month.

This is exactly the kind of review a Banking & Facility Review is built for: an independent look at existing facilities, covenants and pricing before a seasonal funding decision locks anything in, rather than after. For businesses carrying more than one facility, keeping a disciplined cash flow build alongside the covenant position means the stock-to-sales lag is visible well before it becomes a bank conversation.

A business that is funded confidently through December should not be the same business fielding an unexpected covenant call in the middle of its best trading month. The businesses that avoid it are not the ones with the smallest facilities. They are the ones who know their test date and have already shown the bank what the next six weeks look like, often because a fractional CFO relationship means that forecast already exists, updated and ready, rather than built under pressure. If a facility review or a forecast conversation feels overdue, that is a good reason to book a discovery call before the test date arrives rather than after.

faqs.q: What is a loan covenant and why do Australian banks test it?
faqs.a: A loan covenant is a condition written into a lending facility, usually a leverage, interest cover or current ratio, that the bank checks at set intervals to confirm the business remains within an agreed risk profile. It is a routine part of commercial lending, not a sign of distrust. A Banking & Facility Review is a useful way to see which covenants apply to your facilities and how much headroom currently sits against each one.

faqs.q: Can stocking up for Christmas really cause a bank covenant breach?
faqs.a: It can, and it is more common than most owners expect. Debt drawn to fund stock or capacity shows up in the numbers immediately, while the sales and margin it funds only appear once trading happens and the result is reported. If the test date for the facility falls in that gap, a genuinely strong business can show up temporarily outside its covenant, purely on timing rather than performance.

faqs.q: What happens if my business breaches a bank covenant in Australia?
faqs.a: Most lenders will not call a facility over a single technical breach, particularly when it is explained ahead of time with a clear forecast attached. The usual outcome is a waiver, a temporary adjustment or a conversation about the facility terms. The businesses that find this straightforward are the ones who raise it early rather than waiting for the bank to notice first.

faqs.q: How often do Australian lenders test covenants on SME facilities?
faqs.a: It varies by lender and facility size, but quarterly testing against trailing twelve month figures is common for SME lending, with some facilities tested monthly. Knowing the exact test date for each facility matters more than the frequency, since that single date determines which set of numbers the covenant is measured against.

faqs.q: Should I talk to my bank before drawing down extra funding for Christmas trading?
faqs.a: Yes, particularly if the extra funding is significant relative to the facility size. A short conversation with a forecast attached, before the money is drawn, is almost always better received than an explanation after a covenant test has already been missed. If that conversation feels overdue, it is worth booking a discovery call before the test date arrives.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a leverage covenant and a cash flow covenant?
faqs.a: A leverage covenant compares total debt to EBITDA and reacts to how much has been borrowed relative to earnings. A cash flow covenant, often an interest cover or debt service ratio, looks at whether trading cash flow comfortably services the debt. Seasonal stock funding tends to pressure leverage covenants first, since the debt lands before the cash flow it is meant to generate.

faqs.q: How can a Queensland or NSW business prepare for a covenant test during peak trading?
faqs.a: Start by confirming the exact test date and the ratio it applies to, then model where the numbers will sit on that date given funding already committed. Businesses across Queensland and the broader east coast that build this into their regular reporting rhythm rarely get caught by surprise, because the covenant position is checked long before the bank checks it.
